title: When your worth feels like it depends on something

lessons.title: The rejection

screens.heading: An email arrives
paragraphs: On screen
The rejection
Nina has spent three months developing a proposal for a community arts project.
She imagined somewhere young people could learn to paint and make things together. She spent evenings designing the sessions and persuading local businesses to contribute materials.
This morning, she received a reply from the funding organisation.
Email card
Subject: Community Arts Funding Application
Hi Nina,
Thank you for submitting your proposal. We particularly liked the emphasis on involving young people in designing the activities.
Unfortunately, we can't offer funding in this round.
The project has potential, but the current application doesn't provide enough information about recruitment and costs for us to judge whether the plan is deliverable.
You're welcome to submit a revised proposal for the January round.
Best wishes, Community Projects Team
Interaction: Tap the email to expand the highlighted feedback.
Reveal
Two concerns appear in the email: recruitment and costs. The organisation hasn't approved the current proposal, but it has invited Nina to revise it.
Those are the facts she has been given. Her response to them is about to introduce another question.

screens.heading: The conversation
paragraphs: On screen
Nina's friend Asha has been helping organise the project.
Conversation
Asha: Any news?
Nina: They said no.
Asha: Ah, that sucks. Did they say why?
Nina: Budget and recruitment. Apparently I didn't explain either of them properly.
Asha: We can probably sort that. I've still got the contact list from last month.
Nina: I don't think you understand. I've been telling everyone this project is going to happen.
Asha: I know. You worked really hard on it.
Nina: Exactly. And now they're going to realise I had no idea what I was doing.
Asha starts typing, stops, and then sends:
Asha: Are you free for a call?
Nina reads the message but puts her phone down.
Interaction: Dialogue appears naturally as messages. Learner advances through the exchange at their own pace. Earlier messages can be reopened using "Review conversation".

screens.heading: What changed?
paragraphs: On screen
Two different problems
The funding application has a problem that Nina and Asha might be able to fix.
But Nina seems to be struggling with something else as well.
Question
Which sentence tells you the most about why the rejection feels personally threatening?
Tap the sentence that stands out.
A. "Budget and recruitment. Apparently I didn't explain either of them properly."
B. "I've been telling everyone this project is going to happen."
C. "Now they're going to realise I had no idea what I was doing."
Interaction: Ungraded first observation. Learner chooses a sentence, then sees the explanation.
Reveal for A
This identifies what went wrong with the application. Nina may be disappointed about having missed something important.
But it doesn't yet explain why the rejection might change how she sees herself.
Reveal for B
This adds an important pressure. Nina has made a public commitment, so the rejection may feel embarrassing. Other people's expectations are becoming part of the experience.
There's another sentence that takes the problem further.
Reveal for C
This sentence turns feedback about a proposal into a judgment about Nina's ability.
The organisation questioned whether the plan was sufficiently detailed. Nina is beginning to question whether she is capable of developing the project at all.
The distinction matters because correcting an application and trying to prove that you're a capable person are different tasks.

screens.heading: From an outcome to a verdict
paragraphs: On screen
When one thing starts meaning much more
Imagine that you make a mistake while learning to cook.
You might feel annoyed. Perhaps you've wasted ingredients or disappointed someone who was looking forward to dinner.
Now imagine you begin thinking:
"If I can't even get this right, what does that say about me?"
The mistake hasn't changed, but the meaning you've given it has.
You're no longer only evaluating what happened. You're evaluating yourself through what happened.
This is a useful distinction to recognise.
Interaction: Two cards appear.
Card 1: Evaluating the result
"The recipe didn't work. I need to change the temperature."
Card 2: Evaluating myself
"If I can't make this, I must be useless at everything."
Learner taps both cards. They expand to reveal:
Card 1 reveal
The judgment concerns something specific that can be examined and changed.
Card 2 reveal
The judgment spreads from the task to the person. Solving the practical problem may now feel tied to restoring one's sense of worth.

screens.heading: Introducing contingent self-worth
paragraphs: On screen
The invisible condition
Psychologists use the term contingent self-worth to describe the extent to which someone's sense of personal worth depends on particular achievements, qualities or experiences.
Contingent simply means dependent on something.
For example, a person may feel valuable when other people approve of them, but become deeply self-critical when somebody is disappointed.
Another person may feel worthy when they're achieving more than their peers, but struggle to respect themselves when they fall behind.
The important thing is that the outcome does more than affect their mood. It becomes part of how they judge themselves.
In Nina's case, success with the project may have become closely connected to seeing herself as a capable, worthwhile person.
When the proposal was rejected, she didn't only lose an opportunity. She began to feel that the rejection said something about who she was.
Interaction: Tap "Show me how it works".

screens.heading: Building the first model
paragraphs: On screen
Let's follow what happened
Four cards appear as a simple animated sequence.
1 — Something happened
The funding application was rejected.
2 — Nina gave it a meaning
"They can tell I don't know what I'm doing."
3 — That meaning affected how she felt about herself
She began feeling inadequate and embarrassed.
4 — She changed what she did next
She stopped replying to Asha, even though Asha had offered to help revise the proposal.
Explanation
Notice that the rejection itself doesn't contain the words "you are inadequate".
Those words enter the story when Nina interprets the decision as a judgment about her.
The interpretation makes the rejection feel more threatening. If Nina believes her worth depends on succeeding, asking for help may feel like admitting that she isn't good enough.
That could make the practical problem harder to solve.
Interaction: Tap each card to reveal the next. Then tap "See another possibility".
Alternative path
Nina receives the same email.
She feels disappointed and embarrassed.
She thinks: "I really wanted this to work. We clearly didn't explain the budget well enough."
She calls Asha and begins revising the application.
Follow-up text
The second response doesn't require Nina to enjoy rejection or pretend the project wasn't important.
It allows her to remain disappointed while treating the result as information about the application.

screens.heading: Your first practice
paragraphs: On screen
Which thought changes the task?
Nina has agreed to work on the budget with Asha.
Three thoughts occur to her before they meet.
Which one is most likely to make learning from the feedback difficult?
A. "We'll need to get more accurate cost estimates from the suppliers."
B. "I can't ask Asha to explain the budget. She'll realise I'm not qualified to lead this."
C. "We may need to make the project smaller if the materials cost too much."
Correct answer: B
Feedback for B
The difficulty here isn't simply that Nina feels worried about the budget. She believes needing help would expose something bad about her.
That makes an ordinary part of project planning—asking someone to explain something—feel like a threat to her standing as the person leading the project.
She might avoid asking, even when the information would improve the proposal. Or she might spend much longer trying to work everything out alone.
Her concern about being seen as capable has begun influencing which actions feel available to her.
Feedback for A
Cost estimates are part of the original problem. Nina can investigate them without turning the result into a verdict about her worth.
The challenge would be different if she thought she needed to know every figure immediately or she couldn't respect herself.
Feedback for C
Making the project smaller may be a sensible response to limited funding. It reflects a constraint rather than necessarily a judgment about Nina.
A similar thought could become tangled with self-worth if she believed reducing the project meant she was a failure. But that meaning isn't present in this statement.

screens.heading: A distinction worth keeping
paragraphs: On screen
Caring and depending are different
You can care deeply about something without making your entire opinion of yourself depend on succeeding at it.
A person can want an excellent grade, be upset by a disappointing result and work hard to improve.
Someone else can want the same grade but experience anything less than excellence as evidence that they are not good enough.
Their goals may look identical from the outside.
The difference lies partly in what success and failure mean to them.
Interaction: Sort two statements.
"This matters to me"
"I want to do well because I care about the subject."
"This determines how I see myself"
"If I don't do well, I won't feel like I'm worth much."
Feedback
Both statements can exist in the same person. You might genuinely love a subject and also fear that struggling with it would make you inadequate.
Recognising that mixture is useful. It means you can keep the interest or ambition while examining the extra pressure attached to it.

screens.heading: Lesson conclusion
paragraphs: On screen
What Nina's rejection teaches us
An unsuccessful outcome can affect us in more than one way.
We may lose something we wanted. We may feel disappointed. We may also begin treating the outcome as evidence about our value as a person.
When that happens, the desire to do well can become entangled with the need to feel worthy.
You've now met the central idea of contingent self-worth.
In the next lesson, we'll discover why different people can be vulnerable to completely different kinds of outcomes.
Button: Continue to Lesson 2.

lessons.teachingPurpose: introduce the phenomenon through a recognisable situation, then build the first accurate psychological model.

lessons.title: The invisible rules

screens.heading: What would make you feel worthy?
paragraphs: On screen
The invisible rules
Nina thinks she needs to succeed to feel capable.
But imagine somebody who doesn't care very much about academic success. They might be far more affected by rejection from a friend.
Someone else might be relatively comfortable with rejection but feel terrible when they think they look unattractive.
People can attach their sense of worth to different things.
Many of these expectations operate like private rules.
"If I achieve enough, then I'm good enough."
"If people like me, then I'm acceptable."
"If I never disappoint anyone, then I'm a good person."
We don't necessarily sit down and decide to believe these rules. They can become familiar ways of interpreting what happens to us.

Interaction: Reveal four illustrated doors labelled Achievement, Approval, Appearance and Being a Good Person. The learner chooses which example to explore first. All four are encountered before proceeding.

screens.heading: Achievement
paragraphs: On screen
"I have to do well"
Ishan has always performed well at university.
He recently received a lower grade than expected.
Ishan: I got 58.
Friend: That's disappointing. Can you ask for feedback?
Ishan: I will. But I don't know what I'm doing here if I'm not getting firsts.
Friend: You still passed.
Ishan: That's not the point.
Explanation
Ishan may have important academic goals, and the grade may have real consequences for his plans.
His last sentence introduces another possibility.
If his sense of competence or personal worth depends heavily on exceptional performance, an ordinary setback can feel much larger than a disappointing mark.
Interaction: Tap "What rule might be operating?"
Reveal
"If I'm not among the best, I'm not good enough."
Follow-up
The rule creates a difficult standard. Someone must perform well enough to feel acceptable, and the standard may rise whenever they succeed.

screens.heading: Approval
paragraphs: On screen
"People have to be pleased with me"
Tara sends a message to her friend.
"Sorry again about yesterday. I hope I didn't annoy you."
Her friend replies:
"Honestly, I was a bit frustrated. I'm tired today, though. We can talk tomorrow."
Tara reads the message five times.
She begins thinking about everything she might have done wrong over the past month.
Interaction: Choose the best explanation of what has become threatening.
A. Tara may be concerned that the friendship has been damaged and wants to understand what happened.
B. Tara may be treating her friend's disappointment as evidence that she is an unlikeable person.
C. Tara may be worried that leaving the disagreement unresolved will create another argument tomorrow.
Interaction note: This is a guided investigation, not a forced single-answer personality assessment. A and C are plausible concerns; B best reflects contingent selfworth.
Feedback
All three concerns could occur together.
The contingent self-worth element appears when Tara's judgment of herself becomes dependent on whether her friend approves of her.
This can lead to repeated checking or reassurance seeking. The purpose may be to restore the feeling that she's still acceptable, even before the original disagreement has been understood.
The problem is that relationships naturally include moments of frustration. If every sign of disapproval becomes a verdict on your worth, ordinary disagreements can start feeling dangerous.

screens.heading: Appearance
paragraphs: On screen
"I have to look right"
Leah has been looking forward to a friend's birthday.
She takes a photograph of her outfit before leaving.
After comparing it with pictures online, she becomes unhappy with how she looks.
Leah: I think I'm just staying home.
Friend: You said you liked the outfit earlier.
Leah: I did until I saw the pictures. Everyone else looks so much better.
Friend: Do you want to wear something else?
Leah: I don't think it's the clothes anymore.
Explanation
Leah's concern may involve much more than choosing an outfit.
If feeling attractive plays a major part in whether she feels worthy of attention or inclusion, comparing herself with other people may affect whether she feels comfortable being seen at all.
The birthday hasn't become less meaningful. What has changed is how qualified she feels to participate in it.
Interaction: Compare two thoughts.
"I don't like this photograph." "I don't want anyone seeing me like this."
Feedback
Disliking a photograph is not itself contingent self-worth.
The second thought may signal a larger problem when appearance becomes a condition for feeling acceptable around others.
The distinction becomes clearer when we explore what Leah believes would happen if she attended while feeling unattractive.

screens.heading: Being a good person
paragraphs: On screen
"I must never do anything wrong"
Malik forgot his sister's graduation dinner.
He had promised to be there. His sister was hurt.
Sister: I waited for you. You could've at least called.
Malik: I know. I messed up.
Sister: I don't want a huge explanation. I wanted you there.
Later, Malik thinks:
"I'm selfish. I've always been selfish. People who really love their families don't do things like that."
Explanation
Malik has a genuine responsibility to address. Forgetting the dinner affected someone he cares about.
But feeling responsible for a mistake and deciding that the mistake defines your moral worth are different responses.
A person who depends heavily on seeing themselves as perfectly good may struggle when they behave in ways that conflict with that image.
The discomfort can sometimes motivate repair. It can also become so consuming that the person focuses on proving they are good instead of addressing what happened.
Interaction: Tap the best next focus.
A. Work out why the dinner was missed and what Malik could do to repair the hurt.
B. Establish whether Malik's history proves he is generally selfish.
C. Keep apologising until Malik no longer feels like a bad person.
Best-supported answer: A
Feedback
An apology, a conversation about what happened and a reliable plan for the future can all respond to the actual harm.
Repeatedly trying to feel like a good person may not help his sister. Her hurt remains important even after Malik feels reassured about himself.
This is one reason contingent self-worth can create difficulties around morality: protecting the image of being good can sometimes compete with doing the work of being responsible.

screens.heading: The original research
paragraphs: On screen
Different people, different standards
Researchers have studied several domains in which people may base their sense of worth.
These include academic performance, appearance, approval from others, competition, moral conduct, family love and support, and religious beliefs about being loved or accepted by God.
These aren't seven personality types. A person can depend on several domains at once, and their importance can change across circumstances.
The crucial question is how much success or failure in a particular area influences someone's overall view of themselves.
Interaction: Learner opens optional "Explore the research" drawer.
Research drawer

Crocker and colleagues developed a measure of seven contingencies of self-worth in college students. The original domains are useful for understanding variation in selfevaluation, but they do not exhaust every possible source of worth, and a high score in one domain is not a diagnosis.
Continue
Now let's see how the same outcome can mean different things to different people.

screens.heading: Same event, different meaning
paragraphs: On screen
Two people get the same result
Mia and Rowan are both runners.
They finish fourth and fifth in a local race.
Mia is disappointed. She wanted to beat her previous time.
Rowan is devastated. He feels embarrassed to speak to the other runners.
Mia: I was hoping for better. I think I started too fast.
Rowan: I came fifth. What's the point of calling myself a runner?
Question
What additional detail would most help us understand whether Rowan's worth is tied to his performance?
A. Whether Rowan had trained harder than Mia.
B. Whether Rowan generally judges himself negatively when he fails to place highly.
C. Whether other runners noticed Rowan's finishing position.
Best answer: B
Feedback for B
A repeated connection between performance and self-evaluation would tell us more about Rowan's contingency.
A poor finish can be disappointing for practical reasons. But when people repeatedly use results to decide whether they deserve respect, success and failure can carry an added personal meaning.
Feedback for A
Training effort may explain why Rowan is more disappointed. Someone who has invested considerable effort has more reason to care about the result.
It doesn't tell us whether the result also determines how he evaluates himself.
Feedback for C
Being observed may increase embarrassment. Yet Rowan could feel inadequate even if nobody saw the race.
The important issue is the standard he is using to judge himself.

screens.heading: Discover the condition
paragraphs: On screen
Complete the sentence
Sometimes the quickest way to recognise a self-worth contingency is to finish a sentence:
"I feel okay about myself when..."
Nina might answer:
"...my work is successful."
Tara might answer:
"...nobody is upset with me."
Rowan might answer:
"...I'm one of the best."
Now try another:
"When that doesn't happen, I start thinking..."
Interaction: Optional personal reflection with a choice to use a fictional example instead.
Example completion
"I feel okay about myself when people need me."
"When they don't, I start thinking I have nothing to offer."
Reveal
The first sentence points to a condition under which the person feels secure.
The second reveals what losing that condition may mean to them.
This is not a test of whether the person has healthy or unhealthy self-esteem. It is a way of making a personal rule visible enough to examine.

screens.heading: The distinction that matters
paragraphs: On screen
You don't have to stop valuing things
There is a meaningful difference between valuing an achievement and needing that achievement to feel worthy.
You might value kindness while recognising that you sometimes behave unkindly.
You might value competence while accepting that there are things you haven't learnt.
You might value being loved while understanding that another person's temporary frustration doesn't settle whether you deserve care.
These distinctions become easier when we ask:
"Is this something I care about, or something I believe I must achieve to be acceptable?"
Sometimes the answer is both.
That's where the next lesson begins.
Button: Continue to Lesson 3.

lessons.teachingPurpose: introduce the domains of contingent self-worth, distinguish flexible values from rigid conditions, and teach learners to identify the particular standards shaping self-evaluation.

lessons.title: Why it keeps happening

screens.heading: Back to Nina
paragraphs: On screen
Why it keeps happening
It's Monday afternoon.
Nina has been sitting at her desk for nearly four hours.
She hasn't called the suppliers or worked out the recruitment plan.
Instead, she's changed the title of her proposal seven times.
Asha: How's the budget going?
Nina: Nearly there.
Asha: Have you got the material costs?
Nina: Not yet. I'm making the proposal look more professional first.
Asha: I thought that was the part they already liked.
Nina looks back at her screen.
She knows Asha has a point.
But the thought of sending another proposal that might be rejected makes her stomach tighten.
Interaction: Tap the task the funder actually requested.
Reveal
The funding organisation asked for a stronger budget and clearer recruitment plan.
Nina is spending her time on something that feels safer: improving the presentation.
Why might that happen?

screens.heading: A goal becomes a test
paragraphs: On screen
The task has changed
Nina originally wanted to develop a good community project.
Now the task has acquired another purpose: she wants the next proposal to prove that she's capable.
That creates a problem.
If the proposal succeeds, she may feel relieved and proud.
If it fails, she worries that she will feel inadequate again.
As the emotional stakes rise, trying new things can become harder. Asking a basic question or submitting an imperfect draft may feel risky because it creates another opportunity to feel exposed.
Interaction: Reveal the two goals.
Goal A — Improve the project
Find out what costs need including. Ask for help. Revise the proposal.
Goal B — Protect the image of being capable
Avoid showing uncertainty. Make the proposal look impressive. Delay situations where somebody might judge it.
Explanation
These goals are not always incompatible. A person can improve their work and feel more confident as a result.
But if protecting self-worth begins controlling which risks they take, they may favour actions that help them feel safe over actions that would actually help them learn.

screens.heading: The self-worth loop
paragraphs: On screen
How the cycle builds itself
Let's trace the process in Nina's case.
Step 1: A valued outcome is threatened.
Her proposal is rejected.
Step 2: The result becomes a judgment about herself.
"Maybe I'm not capable enough to lead this."
Step 3: That judgment creates pressure.
She feels embarrassed and becomes anxious about being evaluated again.
Step 4: She tries to protect herself.
She avoids asking questions and focuses on polishing the parts of the proposal she already understands.
Step 5: She gets temporary relief.
She can feel productive without exposing the gaps in her plan.
Step 6: The original problem remains.
The budget is still missing. As the deadline approaches, she feels increasingly behind.
Explanation
The behaviour makes sense when we consider what Nina is trying to escape.
She is avoiding another experience that might make her feel inadequate.
The difficulty is that this avoidance also prevents her from gathering information that could help the project.
Interaction: Assemble the actual Nina-specific events into the correct causal order. Cards initially appear shuffled.

screens.heading: Why relief matters
paragraphs: On screen
The behaviour can feel useful
Imagine Nina decides not to email the funder with a question about their feedback.
Immediately, she feels less anxious.
Nobody can judge the question if she doesn't ask it.
For a few minutes, avoiding the email feels like the right decision.
But tomorrow she still doesn't know what the funder meant.
And she has another day's work to catch up on.
Question
What might encourage Nina to avoid asking questions again?
A. The funder's feedback becomes less important each time she avoids it.
B. Avoiding the question gives immediate relief, even though it creates problems later.
C. Nina discovers that asking questions is unnecessary for developing a successful application.
Best answer: B
Feedback
Relief can reinforce avoidance. If staying away from a feared situation makes someone feel better quickly, they may be more inclined to do the same thing next time.
That doesn't mean they consciously choose to keep themselves stuck.
Their immediate emotional problem has been relieved, while the original practical problem remains unresolved.
If the pattern continues, the person may have fewer opportunities to learn that asking for help can be safe and useful.

screens.heading: The opposite response
paragraphs: On screen
What if Nina works harder instead?
Nina's friend Jonah reacts differently to criticism.
When his work is questioned, he doesn't avoid it. He spends every spare hour trying to improve.
He often gets excellent results.
But he rarely feels satisfied.
Jonah: If I can just get this one right, I'll feel better.
Nina: Didn't you get the highest score last time?
Jonah: Yeah, but that doesn't really count anymore.
Explanation
Contingent self-worth doesn't always look like avoidance.
For some people, the fear of not being good enough produces intense effort.
They work longer, prepare more and set increasingly demanding standards because success promises relief from self-doubt.
The results may genuinely improve. The cost is that success can become something they need to repeat to maintain how they feel about themselves.
Interaction: Compare Nina's avoiding and Jonah's overworking.
Reveal
Nina tries to avoid another threatening judgment.
Jonah tries to guarantee a favourable judgment.
Their behaviours differ, but both could be influenced by needing outcomes to confirm their worth.

screens.heading: When success strengthens the rule
paragraphs: On screen
Why success doesn't always settle it
Jonah receives an excellent grade.
For the rest of the afternoon, he feels fantastic.
He thinks about the result while walking home. He imagines telling his friends and putting it on his CV.
The next morning, another assignment appears.
The feeling of success begins to fade.
He starts worrying about whether he can perform as well again.
Explanation
Success can provide genuine satisfaction and useful encouragement.
But when success also serves as proof of personal worth, the feeling of being good enough may become dependent on maintaining the next result.
The very achievement that relieved Jonah's anxiety can raise the stakes of future failure.
This is why simply succeeding more often may not resolve a self-worth contingency. A person may keep needing fresh evidence that they are acceptable.
Interaction: Two arrows.
Short-term: Achievement → pride and relief. Long-term possibility: Worth depends on achievement → greater pressure around the next result.

screens.heading: What happens to learning?
paragraphs: On screen
Being evaluated can change how we learn
Imagine two students who have made the same mistake.
The first student thinks:
"I need to understand why my answer was wrong."
The second thinks:
"I hope nobody notices I didn't know that."
Both might study harder afterwards.
But their attention is directed toward different problems.
The first wants to understand the material.
The second may be preoccupied with protecting their image of being intelligent.
When the fear of looking inadequate becomes strong enough, it can discourage questions, experimentation and honest engagement with mistakes.
This doesn't mean that caring about achievement prevents learning. The concern is what happens when self-protection becomes more important than understanding.

screens.heading: Choose a point of change
paragraphs: On screen
Where could Nina interrupt the cycle?
Nina has spent the afternoon changing the design of the proposal.
It's now 4:30 pm.
Asha has offered to help with the budget.
Which next step would most directly address what's keeping Nina stuck?
A. Spend another hour improving the proposal's appearance so it feels safer to share.
B. Ask Asha to help list the missing costs, even if Nina feels embarrassed about needing help.
C. Stop working on the proposal and decide whether the rejection means she should give up the project.
Best answer: B
Feedback for B
This addresses the problem Nina has been avoiding.
She doesn't need to resolve every doubt about her abilities before taking the step. She can be embarrassed and still ask a useful question.
If she discovers that Asha is willing to help, she may also gain an experience that challenges the idea that needing support makes her inadequate.
Feedback for A
Improving the appearance might be useful later. But the funder has already identified more important gaps.
If Nina keeps polishing the proposal to avoid exposing uncertainty, the action is unlikely to help her complete the missing work.
Feedback for C
Deciding whether to continue the project can be reasonable if the plan is no longer feasible or worthwhile.
But making that decision primarily because rejection has made Nina feel worthless risks allowing her self-evaluation to determine the future of the project.
First, she needs a clearer picture of the actual problems.

screens.heading: Lesson conclusion
paragraphs: On screen
What keeps the cycle going?
Contingent self-worth can affect what people do when something important is threatened.
Some people withdraw. Others try to work until they can no longer be criticised. Some repeatedly seek reassurance or compare themselves with others.
These responses can bring relief or success in the short term.
But if they make self-worth increasingly dependent on future outcomes, the person may remain vulnerable to the next setback.
The useful question is:
"Am I trying to improve the situation, or am I mainly trying to feel acceptable again?"
You may sometimes be doing both.
Button: Continue to Lesson 4.

lessons.teachingPurpose: teach the causal and self-reinforcing processes through which selfworth contingencies can affect interpretation, emotion, behaviour and future learning.

lessons.title: Where the rules come from

screens.heading: A familiar feeling
paragraphs: On screen
Where the rules come from
Nina is talking to her older sister, Maya, about the rejected proposal.
Maya: Did you tell Mum?
Nina: No. I'll tell her when we've sorted it.
Maya: Why wait?
Nina: Because she'll ask how it happened. Then I'll spend twenty minutes explaining that I'm not completely useless.
Maya: She might just ask whether you can apply again.
Nina: Maybe. I just hate having to tell people when something hasn't worked.
Nina pauses.
Nina: I think I've always been like that.
Interaction: Continue to explore three possible ways expectations can develop.

screens.heading: Learning what earns approval
paragraphs: On screen
What gets noticed can become important
Children pay attention to how the people around them respond.
They may notice that achievements bring enthusiasm, while mistakes bring disappointment. They may learn that certain behaviours make people warmer or more attentive.
Sometimes these experiences encourage useful habits.
A child may feel proud because an adult notices their effort or celebrates their progress.
But there can be another message, especially when affection or approval seems to be withdrawn after failure.
The child may begin to believe that being successful, compliant or impressive is necessary to remain valued.
Over time, that expectation can influence how they judge themselves, even when the people who originally held those expectations are no longer present.
Interaction: Two illustrated moments.
Moment A
A child brings home a disappointing test result.
Their parent says: "Oh, that's frustrating. Do you want to show me where you got stuck?"
Moment B
A child brings home a disappointing test result.
Their parent says: "After everything we've done to help you, this is what you bring home?"
Reveal
Both parents may care about academic performance.

The second response adds a question about the child's obligation to justify the support they've received. If similar reactions are common, achievement may become connected to maintaining approval or avoiding guilt.
One conversation is not enough to establish a person's developmental history. The pattern across experiences matters.

screens.heading: Conditional regard
paragraphs: On screen
When approval has conditions
Researchers use the term conditional regard when someone's warmth or approval depends on whether another person behaves in a desired way.
This can happen through withdrawing affection after an unwanted behaviour.
It can also happen when extra affection and approval are offered mainly after meeting a particular standard.
Consider a child who learns:
"When I get the highest grade, everyone is proud of me."
"When I struggle, people become disappointed and distant."
They may begin approaching academic work with two goals.
They want to learn and succeed.
They also want to preserve the feeling of being valued.
That second goal can create considerable pressure, particularly when success becomes difficult to guarantee.
Interaction: Tap "Why this can last".
Reveal
Expectations experienced repeatedly can become internal rules.
An adult may no longer need somebody else to express disappointment. They may criticise themselves automatically when they fail to meet the old standard.
The outside expectation has, in effect, become part of the way they evaluate themselves.

screens.heading: An expectation can become your own voice
paragraphs: On screen
"I should know better"
When Nina receives criticism, a familiar thought appears:
"I should have known."
She thinks the same thing when she misunderstands instructions, misses a deadline or needs help.
She rarely says it to her friends when they make similar mistakes.
Question
What would help Nina explore where this expectation comes from?
A. Consider when the thought first became familiar and what happened when she needed help in the past.
B. Decide which person originally caused her self-worth to become dependent on success.
C. Assume the thought reflects a permanent personality characteristic.
Best answer: A
Feedback
A repeated thought may have a history.
Nina might remember being praised for independence, being criticised for mistakes, or learning that competent people weren't supposed to need help.
Looking at those experiences can help her understand why the expectation feels so convincing.
But remembering a possible influence is different from establishing one definitive cause. Many experiences can reinforce the same belief over time.

screens.heading: School, work and wider expectations
paragraphs: On screen
The environment matters too
Not every self-worth rule begins in the family.
Consider somebody working in an organisation where employees are publicly ranked every month.
Their manager praises the top performers and pays little attention to everybody else.
A person who initially enjoyed the work may gradually begin using their position on the ranking to judge how capable they are.
Or imagine somebody who has repeatedly been criticised for their appearance.
They may become particularly sensitive to whether other people seem to find them attractive.
These experiences matter because people's beliefs about themselves develop within social environments.
Sometimes the pressure isn't imagined. It reflects real consequences attached to other people's judgments.
Interaction: Explore two situations.
Workplace
"Only the highest-rated employees are considered for promotion."
Social setting
"People regularly make jokes about anyone who looks different."
Reveal
The person may have good reasons to care about performance or appearance in these environments.
The psychological question is how those pressures become connected to their broader sense of personal worth—and how they affect their choices.

screens.heading: A rule that once helped
paragraphs: On screen
Why some rules are difficult to give up
Imagine that a person grows up receiving praise for being independent.
They learn to prepare carefully and solve problems alone.
Those habits help them succeed at school and work.
Eventually, they start believing that needing help means they aren't capable.
The original habit still has benefits.
The difficulty appears when the person can no longer choose when independence is useful and when support would be better.
A self-worth rule can feel convincing partly because it has rewarded the person before.
Changing the rule may feel like risking the very thing that helped them succeed.
Interaction: Select the benefit and cost in a short example.
Example: "I have to manage everything alone."
Possible benefit: Strong independent problem-solving skills.
Possible cost: Avoiding useful support when overwhelmed.
Feedback
The aim isn't to erase the person's strengths. It's to give them more flexibility in how they use those strengths.

screens.heading: Understanding Nina without inventing her history
paragraphs: On screen
What do we actually know?
Nina dislikes telling people when she hasn't succeeded.
She expects criticism and avoids asking for help.
Her sister suggests Nina has reacted this way for a long time.
Which explanation is best supported?
A. Nina's current reactions may have been shaped by past expectations, and we need more information to understand them.
B. Nina must have experienced harsh parenting, since she fears criticism.
C. Nina's current workplace is responsible for all her difficulties with failure.
Best answer: A
Feedback
Several pathways could contribute to Nina's reactions.
Her history may matter. Current expectations may matter too. Her own standards, previous setbacks and the importance of the project could all influence the experience.
Understanding where a rule may have come from can make it easier to recognise. But the person doesn't need a complete explanation of its origins before beginning to respond differently.

screens.heading: An optional look back
paragraphs: On screen
A question worth considering
Think of a standard you feel particularly strongly about.
Perhaps it concerns achievement, being helpful, appearance, independence or being liked.
Can you remember when meeting that standard first became especially important?
What happened when you succeeded?
What happened when you didn't?
You can write something down, choose a fictional example, or simply continue.
Interaction: Optional journal or skip.
Reveal after submission
A useful observation might be: "I learnt that being dependable brought approval, and I still feel ashamed when I need support."
That doesn't establish why the expectation developed, but it identifies a connection worth examining.

screens.heading: Lesson conclusion
paragraphs: On screen
A rule can have a history
Our expectations about ourselves can develop through repeated experiences with other people.
They can also be influenced by school, work, social comparison and the standards we repeatedly practise.
Some rules begin as useful ways of succeeding or belonging.
Over time, they may become difficult to question because failure starts feeling like a threat to personal worth.
Knowing this can help explain why changing a familiar expectation may be difficult, even when someone recognises that it has costs.
Button: Continue to Lesson 5.

lessons.teachingPurpose: explain the development and maintenance of self-worth contingencies without reducing them to childhood experiences or assuming one causal origin.

lessons.title: The hidden costs

screens.heading: The missed birthday
paragraphs: On screen
The hidden costs
Asha is getting ready for her birthday dinner.
Nina promised she'd come.
Ten minutes before everyone is due to meet, Asha receives a message.
Nina: Sorry. I don't think I'm going to make it.
Asha: Seriously?
Nina: I need to finish this application.
Asha: You've been saying that all week.
Nina: I know. I'm really sorry.
Asha: I wanted you there, Nina.
Nina puts her phone face down.
She feels terrible about disappointing Asha.
But she opens her laptop again.
Interaction: Continue story.

screens.heading: When a goal takes over
paragraphs: On screen
The project matters. So does the rest of her life.
Nina genuinely cares about the community project.
Finishing the application is important.
But something has changed in the way she's approaching it.
The work no longer feels like a project she wants to improve.
It feels like something she must succeed at before she can relax or enjoy anything else.
She has started postponing sleep, avoiding friends and spending hours on details she previously considered unimportant.
Explanation
Contingent self-worth can make certain goals unusually difficult to set aside.
When success is tied to feeling acceptable, stopping may feel irresponsible or threatening.
The person may keep working even when the extra effort is no longer productive.
The costs often appear outside the original goal.
Interaction: Tap the areas affected in Nina's week: project progress, sleep, friendship and opportunities for learning.

screens.heading: Working hard or trying to prove something?
paragraphs: On screen
They can look similar
Two people are preparing for an important interview.
Person A: "I want to prepare carefully. This role matters to me."
Person B: "I can't afford to look unprepared. If they reject me, I'll feel like I'm not good enough for anything."
Both may spend the evening practising.
The difference becomes clearer when they need to rest.
Person A decides they have prepared enough.
Person B keeps going because stopping brings back the fear of being inadequate.
Question
What best distinguishes the two patterns?
A. Person A is more likely to perform well because they care less.
B. Person B's preparation may be partly driven by the need to prevent a painful judgment about themselves.
C. Person B necessarily has greater motivation because they are more anxious.
Best answer: B
Feedback
The amount of effort alone doesn't tell us whether self-worth is involved.
Person B may be motivated partly by avoiding the feeling of inadequacy. This could make stopping difficult even when further practice has diminishing benefits.
Person A may care just as much about the interview but have more freedom to decide when preparation is sufficient.
The interview can remain important without becoming a test of personal value.

screens.heading: Comparison
paragraphs: On screen
When another person's success feels personal
Asha tells Nina that their friend Finn has received funding for his project.
Asha: Finn got the youth centre grant.
Nina: Oh. Good for him.
Asha: You don't sound very happy.
Nina: No, I am. I just don't understand why his got accepted.
She opens his project page and starts comparing the proposals.
For the next hour, she searches for reasons his application was considered better.
Explanation
Comparison can sometimes provide useful information.
Nina might learn that Finn presented clearer cost estimates or had a more realistic recruitment schedule.
But comparison can also become an attempt to work out where she stands as a person.
If another person's achievement makes Nina feel less capable or less valuable, the comparison may become emotionally threatening even when both people can succeed.
Interaction: Choose the question that best distinguishes useful comparison from selfworth comparison.
A. "What did Finn include that could strengthen our proposal?"
B. "Why did he succeed when I'm supposed to be good at this?"
Feedback
The first question seeks information about the application.
The second connects Finn's success to Nina's view of herself.
Both questions might occur together. The distinction helps us recognise which part is useful for the project and which part is increasing Nina's personal distress.

screens.heading: Reassurance
paragraphs: On screen
"Do you still think I'm capable?"
After the funding rejection, Nina asks Asha:
Nina: Do you actually think I can do this?
Asha: Yeah. You've done loads of good work.
Nina: I just feel like I keep letting everyone down.
Asha: I don't think you are.
Nina feels better for a while.
Later that evening, she starts worrying again.
She considers messaging Asha to ask whether she really meant what she said.
Explanation
Reassurance can be valuable. We sometimes need encouragement, perspective or comfort from people we trust.
But if someone repeatedly uses reassurance to settle whether they are acceptable, the relief may depend on receiving another favourable judgment.
When doubt returns, they may feel compelled to ask again.
The question becomes whether reassurance is helping the person understand and cope with the situation, or whether it is becoming the only way they can feel secure about themselves.

screens.heading: When mistakes threaten identity
paragraphs: On screen
A mistake becomes difficult to admit
Nina discovers that she accidentally left a volunteer's contribution out of the proposal.
The volunteer, Alex, asks her to correct it.
Alex: I don't mind you being the main contact. I just want my work mentioned.
Nina: Of course. I thought I'd included you.
Alex: You hadn't. That's why I'm asking.
Nina feels a sharp wave of embarrassment.
She prides herself on being fair and considerate.
For a moment, she wants to explain all the reasons she didn't mean to leave Alex out.
Question
What would most directly address Alex's concern?
A. Explain that Nina has always cared about giving other people credit.
B. Correct the contribution record and let Alex know what was changed.
C. Ask Alex to reassure Nina that he doesn't think she's selfish.
Best answer: B
Feedback
Nina's wish to be seen as fair is understandable. Being accused of overlooking someone else's work is uncomfortable.
But Alex has asked for a specific correction.
Explaining her good intentions may help later, particularly if there has been a misunderstanding. It doesn't replace the correction.
This illustrates how the need to preserve a positive view of ourselves can sometimes compete with the practical work required after a mistake.

screens.heading: The cost isn't always obvious
paragraphs: On screen
What gets lost?
Imagine somebody who never submits a creative project unless they believe it will receive praise.
Their work may be excellent.
But they may abandon unusual ideas because those ideas could be criticised.
Imagine somebody who works hard to be liked by everyone.
They may become considerate and attentive.
But they may also struggle to express disagreement, even when something matters to them.
The very standards that motivate people can influence which experiences they allow themselves to have.
Interaction: Match the rule to the possible cost.
"I must always look competent." → Avoiding questions or difficult learning opportunities.
"I must never disappoint anyone." → Agreeing to things that exceed personal capacity.
"I must always be the best." → Treating peers' success as threatening.
"I must always be a good person." → Becoming defensive when somebody raises a genuine mistake.
Feedback
These are possible patterns, not inevitable consequences. What matters is whether the rule repeatedly narrows the person's choices.

screens.heading: A difficult choice
paragraphs: On screen
Nina has one evening left
The revised proposal is nearly complete.
Nina still needs to check the material costs.
Asha has invited her to dinner, and Nina has already missed two plans.
What should she do?
A. Spend the entire evening working because another rejection would be too painful.
B. Set aside an hour to confirm the remaining costs, then attend dinner if the proposal is ready to submit.
C. Leave the costs unchecked because personal relationships should always take priority over achievement.
Best-supported answer: B, given the information available.
Feedback
Nina has a genuine responsibility to complete the budget. It would make little sense to abandon essential work simply to prove that achievement no longer matters.
But she also has reason to question whether more work is actually necessary.
A specific task and stopping point allow her to pursue the goal while limiting the extent to which anxiety controls the evening.
If the deadline or work remaining were different, the best decision could change.
The point is to make a decision based on the demands of the situation rather than the need to feel worthy.

screens.heading: Lesson conclusion
paragraphs: On screen
When protecting your worth becomes expensive
Contingent self-worth can make people work hard and care deeply about what they do.
It can also make setbacks feel threatening and success difficult to enjoy.
The costs may appear in the form of avoidance, repeated reassurance, overworking or difficulty acknowledging mistakes.
These patterns become particularly important when they interfere with learning, relationships or the person's ability to make flexible decisions.
In the next lesson, we'll look at what someone can actually do when a result starts feeling like a verdict on them.
Button: Continue to Lesson 6.

lessons.teachingPurpose: show how the pursuit and protection of self-worth can affect learning, relationships, motivation and decision-making.

lessons.title: Changing your relationship with failure

screens.heading: Another setback
paragraphs: On screen
What happens when the feeling returns?
Nina and Asha have completed the revised proposal.
They send it to a colleague for feedback.
The colleague replies:
"The budget looks clearer, but I think the recruitment section needs another revision. I'm not sure the numbers are realistic."
Nina feels her stomach drop.
Her first thought is familiar:
"I'm still not good enough at this."
This time, before changing anything, she opens her notebook.
Interaction: Tap the notebook.

screens.heading: Separate the result from the verdict
paragraphs: On screen
What happened? What did I conclude?
Nina writes two sentences.
What happened
"The colleague thinks the recruitment estimate is unrealistic."
What I concluded about myself
"I'm not capable enough to lead the project."
She looks at them side by side.
The first sentence describes feedback she can investigate.
The second makes a broader judgment about her competence.
Explanation
Separating these statements doesn't mean the colleague is wrong.
Nina may genuinely need to revise her recruitment plan. Perhaps she has overlooked important information.
The distinction allows her to take the feedback seriously without automatically accepting every negative conclusion that comes into her mind.
Interaction: Learner sorts four statements into "Feedback about the task" or "Judgment about the person".
"The recruitment estimate needs more evidence." → Task.
"I don't deserve to lead anything." → Person.
"We need to contact the schools before estimating attendance." → Task.
"Other people would have done this properly." → Person.
Feedback
Once we can see the difference, we can ask whether each statement has useful evidence behind it.
The goal is to evaluate the task accurately while avoiding conclusions that go further than the information supports.

screens.heading: A different question
paragraphs: On screen
What would actually help?
Nina could spend the next hour arguing with herself about whether she's capable.
She could search for reassurance from Asha.
She could also contact two schools and ask whether the proposed recruitment numbers are realistic.
Only one of those actions directly answers the question raised in the feedback.
Interaction: Tap the action that gives Nina new information.
Reveal
Contacting the schools gives Nina evidence she currently lacks.
She may discover that the estimate was too high and needs changing.
She may discover that it was reasonable but poorly explained.
Either outcome would help her improve the proposal.
Explanation
When self-worth feels threatened, an important practical skill is to recover the original problem.
What actually happened?
What can be learnt?
What action would make the situation clearer?
Those questions can help a person choose what to do while still experiencing disappointment or embarrassment.

screens.heading: Why being kinder to yourself can help
paragraphs: On screen
A mistake doesn't require self-punishment
Some people worry that if they stop criticising themselves, they'll become complacent.
They believe harsh self-judgment is what makes them improve.
But consider what happens when someone makes a mistake and feels too ashamed to look at it properly.
They may avoid the feedback, become defensive or give up.
Responding with greater understanding can sometimes make it easier to face the mistake and take responsibility for it.
Self-compassion means acknowledging that you're struggling and treating yourself with reasonable care, while remaining willing to examine what happened.
It doesn't require pretending that the mistake was harmless or that everything is fine.
Interaction: Compare two responses after a disappointing result.
Response A
"I'm such an idiot. I always ruin things. I need to get my act together."
Response B
"I'm disappointed. I can see why this happened, and I need to understand what to change."
Reveal
Response B leaves more room to investigate the specific problem.
It acknowledges disappointment and responsibility without turning the event into a broad personal attack.
This can be particularly useful when shame or self-criticism is making someone avoid the work needed to improve.

screens.heading: Build a useful response
paragraphs: On screen
Help Nina answer the feedback
Nina wants to send a message to her colleague.
Choose the reply that would help her understand what needs changing.
A. "I've worked hard on this and I think the recruitment numbers are fair. I don't really want to redo the plan again."
B. "Thanks for checking this. Could you point out which assumptions seem unrealistic? I'll compare them with the school contact list before revising."
C. "You're right. I shouldn't have sent this until it was completely ready. I'll start the entire proposal again."
Best answer: B
Feedback for B
Nina asks for the information needed to evaluate the criticism.
She doesn't automatically reject it, and she doesn't assume the whole project is worthless because one section needs improving.
The reply gives her a manageable next step.
Feedback for A
Nina may be right that she has worked hard. But effort doesn't establish whether the recruitment numbers are realistic.
Her response protects the existing plan without finding out whether it needs changing.
Feedback for C
Nina accepts the criticism, but she responds more broadly than the feedback warrants.
The colleague questioned the recruitment assumptions. Restarting the entire proposal could waste work that is already sound.

screens.heading: A small experiment
paragraphs: On screen
Practise being imperfect without giving up
Imagine you usually delay asking for help until you've tried everything yourself.
The next time you get stuck on something small, you could try asking a clear question earlier than usual.
Before doing so, write down what you're worried might happen.
For example:
"If I ask this question, they'll think I shouldn't be doing the job."
Then notice what actually happens.
Perhaps the person answers normally. Perhaps they are busy or unsure themselves. Perhaps the question reveals a genuine skill gap that needs attention.
The aim is to gather information about what happens when you act without first securing the feeling of being completely capable.
Interaction: Build a small experiment.
Example
Situation: I don't understand a requirement in my assignment.
Feared meaning: If I ask, the tutor will think I'm unintelligent.
Action: Ask one specific question about the requirement.
What I will observe: How the tutor responds and whether the answer helps me understand the task.
Review: Did my feared judgment occur? What else did I learn?
Feedback
A useful experiment is specific enough that you can actually complete it.
Choose something proportionate to your circumstances. The purpose is to test an expectation rather than force yourself into an unnecessarily high-stakes situation.

screens.heading: Failure can still matter
paragraphs: On screen
You can be disappointed and keep your perspective
There is no need to deny the consequences of failure.
A poor grade can affect an application. An unsuccessful interview can delay a career move. A mistake can harm somebody else.
Those consequences deserve attention.
But they don't automatically justify a judgment about the whole person.
Imagine telling a friend:
"You didn't get the job. That means you should reconsider how you prepared."
Now compare it with:
"You didn't get the job. That means you're not a worthwhile person."
The second conclusion doesn't follow from the first.
It adds a judgment about personal worth that the event itself cannot establish.
Interaction: Choose the statement that best preserves both responsibility and perspective.
A. "This result is meaningless, so there's nothing to learn."
B. "This result matters, and I can examine what it tells me without using it to judge my entire worth."
C. "I need to succeed next time before I can feel okay about myself."
Best answer: B
Feedback
This response allows disappointment and learning to coexist.
It also weakens the assumption that a favourable outcome is required before the person can regard themselves with respect.

screens.heading: Responding to the familiar thought
paragraphs: On screen
"I'm not good enough"
Nina notices the thought returning.
Instead of trying to force herself to believe the opposite, she asks:
"What does 'good enough' mean here?"
Good enough to be accepted by the funder?
Good enough to lead the project?
Good enough to deserve respect from her friends?
Those are different questions.
The funder may have specific standards Nina needs to meet.
Her competence can be developed and evaluated.
Her worth as a person doesn't need to be settled every time somebody assesses her work.
Interaction: Learner selects one of three ways of responding to the thought.
Option A — Challenge its accuracy
"What evidence do I have that this one result describes my abilities generally?"
Option B — Change its meaning
"I can struggle with this task without making it a judgment about everything I am."
Option C — Return to action
"What is one useful thing I can do about the actual problem?"
Feedback
Different responses may be useful at different times.
If the thought rests on an inaccurate conclusion, examining the evidence can help.
If the person already knows the thought is exaggerated but remains emotionally caught by it, changing their relationship to the thought may matter more.
If they are stuck in repeated self-evaluation, returning to a concrete action may be particularly useful.

screens.heading: Make a plan for the next time
paragraphs: On screen
A plan for an uncomfortable moment
Think of a situation where you sometimes feel that your worth is being tested.
You can prepare a simple response before the next setback occurs.
Step 1
"When this happens..."
Example: "When somebody criticises my work."
Step 2
"I tend to conclude..."
Example: "That I'm not capable enough."
Step 3
"What I can examine instead..."
Example: "Which part of the work needs improving."
Step 4
"One action I can take..."
Example: "Ask for one specific piece of feedback."
Interaction: Sentence builder with editable fields, optional save to Field Guide, and a worked example for those who do not want to write about themselves.
Feedback
The plan doesn't need to eliminate the uncomfortable feeling.
It needs to help you make a useful choice while the feeling is present.

screens.heading: Lesson conclusion
paragraphs: On screen
Learning without putting yourself on trial
Changing contingent self-worth doesn't require abandoning your ambitions or ignoring criticism.
It involves becoming more flexible about what outcomes mean.
You can evaluate a mistake without making it the measure of your entire character.
You can learn from disappointment without punishing yourself for experiencing it.
You can take a useful action before you feel completely confident.
Next, we'll examine a particularly difficult area: what happens when your sense of worth depends on another person's approval.
Button: Continue to Lesson 7.

lessons.teachingPurpose: teach an actionable response to self-worth threats that preserves ambition, accurately evaluates outcomes and supports flexible behaviour.

lessons.title: Worth in relationships

screens.heading: Asha has had enough
paragraphs: On screen
When somebody is disappointed in you
Asha asks Nina to meet after work.
Asha: Can I say something without you immediately apologising?
Nina: That's not a promising start.
Asha: You've cancelled on me three times. I know the project is stressful, but I feel like I only see you when you need help with it.
Nina goes quiet.
Nina: I didn't realise you felt like that.
Asha: I know you haven't meant to hurt me. But it still hurts.
Nina looks away.
Nina: I'm a terrible friend.
Asha: That's not what I said.
Interaction: Tap to continue.

screens.heading: When criticism becomes a verdict
paragraphs: On screen
What is Asha asking for?
Asha is telling Nina that their friendship has been affected by her behaviour.
Nina immediately begins thinking about whether she is a good friend at all.
That changes the conversation.
Asha wants the missed plans acknowledged and something to improve.
Nina is now distressed by the possibility that she may be a bad person.
Interaction: Select the sentence that most clearly introduces a judgment about Nina's identity.
A. "You've cancelled on me three times."
B. "I feel like I only see you when you need help with the project."
C. "I'm a terrible friend."
Best answer: C
Feedback
Asha describes a repeated behaviour and its effect on her.
Nina responds by drawing a broad conclusion about herself.
Her distress may be sincere. But if the conversation becomes entirely about reassuring Nina that she's a good friend, Asha's original concern could remain unaddressed.
This is one way a need to preserve self-worth can complicate accountability.

screens.heading: Approval and belonging
paragraphs: On screen
Why other people's opinions matter
Humans are social. Our relationships can have enormous practical and emotional significance.
Being criticised or rejected by somebody we care about can genuinely hurt.
Wanting approval and belonging is not inherently a problem.
The difficulty arises when somebody else's response becomes a measure of whether we are an acceptable person.
Imagine thinking:
"My friend is frustrated with something I did."
Now imagine thinking:
"My friend is frustrated, so there must be something fundamentally wrong with me."
The second thought adds a judgment that may make it harder to address the disagreement.
Interaction: Compare the emotional and practical implications of both interpretations.
Reveal
When criticism concerns a specific behaviour, there may be room to apologise, explain or negotiate.
When criticism is experienced as proof of personal inadequacy, the person may become preoccupied with defending their worth or restoring reassurance.

screens.heading: Asha's side matters
paragraphs: On screen
Nina isn't the only person in the conversation
Asha has a real complaint.
Nina has repeatedly cancelled plans.
If the lesson only helped Nina feel better about herself, it would miss something important.
A useful response has to make room for Asha's experience too.
Question
Which response would most directly address the friendship problem?
A. "I know I've been a terrible friend. I can't believe I've let you down again."
B. "I didn't realise how often I'd cancelled. I'm sorry. I want to make more time for us, and I need to be realistic about when I can commit."
C. "I've had a lot going on. You should understand why I haven't been available."
Best answer: B
Feedback
Nina acknowledges the behaviour and its impact.
She also recognises that making another promise she can't keep would probably make matters worse.
The response is practical because it allows the friendship to change.
A long declaration of how terrible she feels might be sincere, but it doesn't tell Asha whether anything will improve.

screens.heading: What if approval really is conditional?
paragraphs: On screen
Sometimes the pressure comes from someone else
Not every fear of losing approval is an inaccurate interpretation.
Imagine somebody whose partner repeatedly becomes cold and distant whenever they express disagreement.
Eventually, they may begin avoiding ordinary disagreements because they expect affection to be withdrawn.
Their behaviour isn't necessarily explained by a private self-worth rule alone.
The relationship may also be teaching them that expressing their needs carries a cost.
Interaction: Compare two situations.
Situation A
A partner says, "I felt hurt by what happened. I'd like us to talk about it."
Situation B
A partner says, "If you disagree with me about this, don't expect me to be affectionate with you."
Reveal
The first statement expresses hurt and invites a conversation.
The second makes affection conditional on agreement.
Understanding the difference matters because the practical response depends partly on how the other person behaves.
Learning to value yourself more securely doesn't require pretending that harmful treatment is acceptable.

screens.heading: Caring without surrendering yourself
paragraphs: On screen
You can care about somebody's feelings and still have limits
Imagine a friend asks you for help every evening.
You want to support them.
But you're exhausted and need time to rest.
If your self-worth depends on always being helpful, saying no may make you feel selfish.
Yet agreeing to every request may leave you resentful and less available when you genuinely want to help.
Interaction: Construct a response from three possible messages.
Option A
"I'm sorry. I know you need me. I'll stay up if that's what you want."
Option B
"I care about you, but I can't stay up tonight. I can talk tomorrow afternoon."
Option C
"You rely on me too much. You need to stop asking."
Best-supported response: B, for the stated circumstances.
Feedback
This response takes the other person's need seriously without making unlimited availability the condition of being a caring friend.
The limit is clear, and it includes an alternative.
Sometimes the other person will feel disappointed. That feeling doesn't automatically establish that the boundary was wrong.
Equally, a boundary should not be used to dismiss responsibilities that somebody has already agreed to.
The relevant question is what the person can reasonably offer and what they have actually committed to.

screens.heading: When being good becomes a performance
paragraphs: On screen
Doing good things and needing to feel good are different
Imagine someone who volunteers regularly.
They enjoy helping people and care about their community.
One day, they make a mistake that inconveniences another volunteer.
They feel ashamed and begin repeatedly explaining how much they usually contribute.
The desire to be seen as a good person has become more urgent than addressing the mistake.
A more useful response might be:
"I can see the problem I caused. What needs putting right?"
This allows the person to take responsibility without first proving that they deserve to think well of themselves.
Interaction: Learner chooses between two priorities.
Protect the identity: Establish that I'm normally a considerate person.
Address the effect: Understand what happened and make a suitable correction.
Feedback
These goals may both matter emotionally.
But the second is usually more relevant to the person affected by the mistake.
A positive moral identity can support prosocial behaviour. Difficulties arise when maintaining that identity interferes with acknowledging what actually happened.

screens.heading: Returning to Asha
paragraphs: On screen
An honest conversation
Later, Nina messages Asha.
Nina: I've been thinking about what you said.
Asha: Okay.
Nina: You're right that I've cancelled a lot. I don't think I realised how much I was pushing everything else aside.
Asha: I was starting to wonder if you even wanted to see me.
Nina: I do. I've just been so focused on getting the proposal right that I haven't left room for much else.
Asha: I get that. I just don't want another plan that gets cancelled at the last minute.
Nina: That's fair. Can we pick a day after the deadline? I'll make sure I'm actually free before promising.
Asha agrees to arrange something for the following weekend.
Explanation
Nina hasn't needed to prove that she's a perfect friend.
She's acknowledged the effect of her behaviour and made a more realistic commitment.
Asha may still feel disappointed for a while. The conversation doesn't need to erase that immediately.
Repair can involve allowing another person to have their feelings while taking practical steps to improve the relationship.

screens.heading: Lesson conclusion
paragraphs: On screen
Your worth and your relationships
Other people's responses affect us because relationships matter.
When someone's approval becomes a condition for feeling acceptable, ordinary disagreements can become unusually threatening.
But not every relationship difficulty is caused by contingent self-worth.
Sometimes a person has behaved in a way that needs addressing. Sometimes the environment places unreasonable conditions on approval or belonging.
Understanding the difference can help us respond more accurately.
We can acknowledge mistakes, care about other people and set reasonable limits without needing every interaction to confirm our worth.
Button: Continue to the final lesson.

lessons.teachingPurpose: distinguish legitimate relational needs from worth-contingent selfevaluation; address conditional approval, accountability and context-sensitive boundaries.

lessons.title: Taking it into real life

screens.heading: A different situation
paragraphs: On screen
Can you recognise the pattern elsewhere?
You've followed Nina through the funding application, her attempts to improve it and the effects on her relationships.
Now we're leaving her story.
The next situations involve people you haven't met.
You'll need to decide what is happening using the evidence available, rather than relying on familiar wording.
Some cases involve contingent self-worth.
Others involve ordinary disappointment, reasonable concern or real external pressures.
Button: Begin investigation.

screens.heading: Case One: The examination
paragraphs: On screen
Case One — The examination
Amir has been preparing for a professional qualification.
He is applying for a competitive graduate role, and passing the examination would strengthen his application.
He fails by four marks.
Amir: I knew that paper went badly.
Friend: You've still got another chance to take it.
Amir: That's not the point. Everyone thought I was going to do well.
Friend: You'll need to change how you revise, but this isn't the end.
Amir: I don't know how I'm supposed to respect myself when I can't even pass this.
Question
What evidence most directly suggests that Amir's self-worth is involved?
A. The qualification has practical consequences for his career.
B. Other people expected him to do well, which makes the failure embarrassing.
C. He connects failing the exam to whether he can respect himself.
Best answer: C
Feedback
The exam matters for several reasons. Amir has a career goal, and failure may delay it.
His embarrassment is understandable too.
The strongest evidence of contingent self-worth is his statement that failing affects whether he can respect himself.
That moves beyond the exam's practical consequences and makes achievement a condition for his self-evaluation.

screens.heading: Case One: What would help?
paragraphs: On screen
Amir has another examination in six weeks.
He needs to decide how to prepare.
Three possibilities are suggested.
A. Study every available hour so that he cannot feel this way again.
B. Analyse which areas he missed, develop a revised study plan and allow time for rest.
C. Avoid taking the examination again until he feels completely confident.
Best-supported answer: B
Feedback
Amir needs to improve his preparation. The first failure may reveal genuine gaps in his understanding.
But organising all his behaviour around preventing another blow to self-worth could make preparation harder to sustain.
A realistic study plan allows him to work toward passing while treating mistakes as information about what needs attention.

screens.heading: Case Two: The disagreement
paragraphs: On screen
Case Two — The disagreement
Sophie and her partner have been arguing more often.
After a disagreement about weekend plans, her partner says:
"I'm frustrated because you changed the arrangement without asking me."
Sophie begins thinking:
"If they're frustrated with me, maybe I'm impossible to be with."
She spends the rest of the evening trying to persuade her partner that she's a good person.
Question
Which element of the situation is most relevant to contingent self-worth?
A. Sophie is upset because she has been criticised by someone important to her.
B. Sophie has begun interpreting a specific disagreement as evidence that she may be fundamentally unsuitable as a partner.
C. Sophie wants to understand why her partner was upset about the changed plans.
Best answer: B
Feedback
Sophie is taking a specific conflict and using it to evaluate herself more broadly.
The disagreement concerns an arrangement that was changed without consultation.
Her reaction suggests that being seen positively by her partner may be closely connected to feeling acceptable in the relationship.
If the conversation becomes centred on proving she is a good partner, the original disagreement may be harder to resolve.

screens.heading: Case Two: New information
paragraphs: On screen
A new detail changes the picture
You learn that Sophie's partner regularly says:
"If you loved me properly, you'd always do things my way."
When Sophie disagrees, the partner sometimes refuses to speak to her for several days.
Question
How should this information change your understanding?
A. Sophie's self-worth concerns may still matter, but the partner's behaviour also creates a real pressure around disagreement.
B. Sophie's feelings are entirely caused by the partner, so her own interpretations are irrelevant.
C. The relationship difficulty is mostly a problem of Sophie having low self-esteem.
Best answer: A
Feedback
The new information changes the context.
Sophie's fear of disapproval may be reinforced by her partner's conditional demands.
Working on her self-evaluation could help her recognise that disagreement doesn't make her unworthy of care.
But the relationship's actual conditions also need attention. An explanation focused only on Sophie's thoughts would miss the pressure created by the partner's behaviour.

screens.heading: Case Three: The apology
paragraphs: On screen
Case Three — The apology
Oliver makes an insensitive joke during a family gathering.
His sister tells him it was hurtful.
Oliver becomes upset.
Oliver: I was only joking. I can't believe you think I'd deliberately hurt you.
Sister: I'm not saying you meant to. I'm saying it upset me.
Oliver: I'm a good brother. I've always tried to be there for you.
Sister: I know. I just wish you'd listen to why it bothered me.
Question
What is happening in this exchange?
A. Oliver is trying to establish that his overall intentions are good, while his sister is asking him to acknowledge a specific effect of his behaviour.
B. Oliver is entitled to defend himself because his sister cannot know what he intended.
C. The disagreement can only be resolved once his sister confirms that Oliver is a good person.
Best answer: A
Feedback
Oliver's intentions matter. If his sister mistakenly believed he meant to hurt her, he may reasonably want to clarify that.
But she has already said she isn't accusing him of deliberate harm.
Her complaint concerns the effect of the joke.
Oliver's concern about being seen as a good brother may be distracting him from what she is trying to explain.
He can acknowledge that she was hurt without agreeing that he intended to hurt her.

screens.heading: Case Four: A justified concern
paragraphs: On screen
Case Four — The performance review
Elena works in a company undergoing redundancies.
Her manager tells her that the quality of her work has recently declined.
Elena feels worried.
She asks for specific examples and wants to know whether the review could affect her employment.
Question
Which conclusion is best supported?
A. Elena's concern about the review is evidence that her self-worth depends on achievement.
B. Elena has a legitimate reason to investigate the criticism because the review may affect her employment.
C. Elena should avoid evaluating her performance because doing so could make her self-esteem dependent on work.
Best answer: B
Feedback
Elena's reaction may be explained by the practical stakes.
A performance review can affect employment, income and future opportunities.
Wanting accurate information about those consequences is sensible.
Elena might also experience contingent self-worth, but nothing in the description establishes that the review has become a verdict on her value as a person.
This case reminds us why context is essential.
Not every strong emotional response to evaluation is evidence of contingent selfworth.

screens.heading: Explain the process yourself
paragraphs: On screen
What have you learnt?
Imagine explaining contingent self-worth to somebody who has never encountered the term.
You have three questions to answer.
1. What does contingent self-worth mean?
2. Why might it make a disappointing result harder to cope with?
3. What could help someone respond differently?
Interaction: Optional written response, or a structured builder for users who prefer guided expression. No automatic psychological scoring.
Self-check model answer
Contingent self-worth occurs when someone's sense of value depends strongly on certain outcomes, such as achievement or other people's approval.
