A setback can become particularly painful because it may be interpreted as evidence that the person isn't good enough. They may then try to restore their worth through overworking, avoiding failure or seeking reassurance.
A useful response involves identifying the specific problem, recognising when it is being turned into a broader self-judgment, and choosing an action that helps with the situation.
Feedback
A complete explanation should include the condition, its effect on self-evaluation and at least one way it can influence behaviour.
It doesn't need technical terminology.

screens.heading: The final decision
paragraphs: On screen
One last situation
You have worked hard on something that matters to you.
You receive criticism.
You feel disappointed and begin thinking that the result might mean you're not capable enough.
Which response would best reflect the understanding developed in this unit?
A. Convince yourself that the criticism doesn't matter, so you can stop feeling disappointed.
B. Accept that the criticism may contain useful information, examine what it tells you about the task and resist turning it into a verdict on your whole self.
C. Work until the criticism has been resolved so you can feel completely confident in yourself again.
Best answer: B
Feedback
You don't have to remove the disappointment before responding.
You can take criticism seriously and work to improve without making your personal worth dependent on achieving a particular result.
That flexibility is the central skill this unit has been building.

screens.heading: Your personal take-away
paragraphs: On screen
One rule you want to loosen
You've seen how success, failure and other people's responses can become conditions for feeling worthy.
You may have recognised one of these conditions in yourself.
Choose one you would like to examine.
Options
"When I fail, I feel inadequate."
"When somebody is disappointed in me, I question whether I'm a good person."
"When somebody else succeeds, I feel less capable."
"When I need help, I feel ashamed."
"Something else."
Interaction: Choose one and complete an optional action plan.
On screen
The next time this happens, I want to remember:
"What happened is something I can examine. I don't need to settle my worth before deciding what to do."
One small action I could try:
[Editable response]

screens.heading: Unit complete
paragraphs: On screen
You've completed your first unit
When your worth feels like it depends on something
You began with Nina's rejected funding application.
You saw how an outcome could become a judgment about the person experiencing it.
You explored different standards that people may attach their worth to and how those standards can develop.
You followed the ways self-worth threats can influence behaviour and learnt practical responses that preserve the importance of goals without making every result a test of personal value.
Most importantly, you practised applying the concept beyond Nina's story.
What you can now do
 Recognise when self-evaluation becomes attached to an outcome.
 Distinguish disappointment about a result from a broader judgment of personal worth.
 Explain how self-worth contingencies can influence behaviour.
 Identify when a competing explanation fits better.
 Choose a proportionate response that keeps learning and practical responsibilities in view.
Closing message
You may still feel deeply disappointed when something important goes wrong.
You may still care what people think about you.
The difference is that you can begin to notice when those experiences are being asked to answer a much larger question about your value.
And when that happens, you have more than one way to respond.

lessons.teachingPurpose: independent transfer, discrimination between plausible interpretations, practical planning and unit consolidation.

screens.heading: Next visit
paragraphs: On screen
Do you remember the distinction?
Two people receive the same disappointing result.
One thinks: "I need to improve my approach."
The other thinks: "This proves I'm not good enough."
What is the most important difference between their interpretations?
Answer choices
A. The second person cares more about succeeding.
B. The second person is using the outcome to evaluate themselves more broadly.
C. The first person is more confident in their abilities.
Best answer: B
Feedback
Both people may care deeply about the result.
The distinction is that the second person has connected the outcome to their sense of worth.
The same event can therefore produce a different psychological response depending on the meaning it carries.

screens.heading: Approximately one week later
paragraphs: On screen
A new situation
A musician makes a mistake during a performance.
For the next week, they avoid rehearsing with other people because they are afraid of being seen as untalented.
What would be a useful first step?
A. Work out what went wrong and choose a manageable opportunity to practise with others.
B. Avoid performing until their confidence has fully returned.
C. Practise privately until they can guarantee that the same mistake will never happen again.
Best answer: A
Feedback
The musician can improve their performance without needing to guarantee that nobody will judge them.
A manageable return to practice allows them to learn while also testing the expectation that making mistakes makes them unacceptable.

screens.heading: Later independent retrieval
paragraphs: On screen
Explain it without a clue
A friend says:
"I know I shouldn't be this upset about one disappointing result, but it makes me feel like everything I've worked for means nothing."
How would you explain what might be happening?
What would you ask before assuming contingent self-worth is the best explanation?
What could help them take their next step?
Interaction: Short written response or structured builder, followed by an authored self-check.
Self-check
A good explanation would consider whether the disappointing result has become connected to the friend's broader sense of worth.
It would also ask what practical consequences the result has and whether the person's distress reflects understandable losses or pressures.
A useful response would preserve the significance of the setback while helping the person distinguish the specific problem from conclusions about their overall value.
End of review.

evidence: Crocker and Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of Self-Worth, and Crocker et al. (2003), Contingencies of Self-Worth in College Students: Theory and Measurement, form the conceptual basis for Lessons 1–2.

Crocker and Park (2004), The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem, informs Lessons 3 and 5. The content distinguishes potentially motivating effects of contingent self-worth from the difficulties that can arise when self-validation dominates learning and decisionmaking.

Assor, Roth and Deci (2004), The Emotional Costs of Parents' Conditional Regard, and the later meta-analytic literature inform Lesson 4. Developmental explanations should remain contextual and should not be treated as a complete account of any particular person's history.

Breines and Chen (2012), Self-Compassion Increases Self-Improvement Motivation, informs Lesson 6. The manuscript uses this evidence to support the possibility that a less punitive response to failure can coexist with genuine motivation to improve.

Crocker and Canevello (2008), Creating and Undermining Social Support in Communal Relationships, informs the distinction between protecting an image of oneself and acting toward relational goals in Lesson 7.

All stories are fictional learning demonstrations. The lessons are authored teaching hypotheses, not validated clinical interventions. The exercise sequence and assessment criteria require user testing before they are treated as evidence of realworld learning or behaviour change.

screens.heading: Welcome
paragraphs: On screen
When your worth feels like it depends on something
Have you ever had a small mistake ruin your entire day?
Perhaps somebody was disappointed in you, an exam didn't go as planned, or you saw another person doing better than you.
You might have felt disappointed, which makes sense. But sometimes the feeling goes further. A disappointing result starts changing how you see yourself.

A mistake becomes evidence that you aren't capable. Somebody's disapproval makes you feel difficult to love. One unsuccessful attempt leaves you questioning whether you have anything worthwhile to offer.
Why can a single event sometimes have so much power over the way we see ourselves?
In this unit, we're going to explore that question.
Interaction: Begin unit.
No question yet. The learner has not been introduced to the concept.

screens.heading: What you'll learn
paragraphs: On screen
By the end of this unit, you'll understand why certain experiences can make your confidence rise or fall so dramatically.
You'll learn to recognise the expectations you've attached to yourself, understand why they can become so powerful, and practise responding to setbacks without allowing them to define you.
You won't be asked to stop caring about what matters to you.
Instead, we'll explore how you can pursue meaningful goals without making every outcome a judgment of your worth.
